title: Steve-O's Wild Ride! #80 — David Choe
summary: Steve-O, David Choe and the Wild Ride crew move from prison, bowel anxiety and Korean identity into recovery, shame, wealth, medical shortcuts, service work and the difficulty of saying no. Three sponsor blocks are structurally separate. Choe and Steve-O describe Japanese custody, drug conditioning, BioXcellerator treatment in Colombia, propofol, pain and John Sarno, but repeatedly mix first-person testimony with unsupported medical and political generalizations. Choe rejects a proposed biohacking package, challenges the richest-artist headline, explains how visible recklessness hides years of practice, and recounts anonymous equine-ranch labor and portraits for women he characterizes as trafficking/abuse survivors. The latter becomes a self-indictment about paid sex and turning addiction into content, not a rescue story. The second half connects The Choe Show, pulled episodes and guest refusal with shame, teenage self-harm/graffiti rituals, wealth anxiety and an unmade survival-reality proposal that Choe ultimately declines. The close separates Choe's projection that Steve-O likes being hated from Steve-O's direct disagreement, then returns to fighting, legacy and DVDASA runtimes. Every idea remains; private women, children, recovery participants, residences, treatment claims, rapid weight loss, self-harm and dangerous conduct are controlled through narrow contextual restrictions rather than deletion. Zero publisher speaker prefixes exist, so named line-level turns remain withheld.

source_notes.claim: Choe is the richest painter on Earth.
source_notes.assessment: This is host promotion, not an audited ranking; Choe later rejects the headline.

source_notes.claim: Known participants make every line safely nameable.
source_notes.assessment: They do not. All 2,653 caption segments contain zero publisher speaker prefixes and include ads, quotations, crew talk, performance and a post-interview wrap.

source_notes.claim: The Colombia procedures are illegal in the U.S. because they threaten pharmaceutical profits.
source_notes.assessment: The causal explanation is speculation. FDA guidance says only limited blood-forming cord-blood stem-cell products are approved in the U.S.; the broad spinal, concussion, facial and whole-body uses described here are not established by this testimony.

source_notes.claim: Steve-O's experience is independent medical evidence.
source_notes.assessment: He explicitly says treatment was free in exchange for posts, a material compensation relationship that must remain visible.
